title: Higher Order Derivatives: From Velocity to Jerk

sections.title: The First Derivative: Rate of Change
sections.teaches: The first derivative represents the instantaneous rate of change (slope) of a function.
sections.visual: A smooth blue curve representing position f(t) appears. A tangent line touches the curve at a moving point; as the point moves right, the angle of the tangent line changes dynamically. Labels 'f(t)' and 'f'(t)' appear near the curve and the slope value respectively.
sections.narration: We begin with position over time. The first derivative gives us velocity—the instantaneous rate at which position is changing. Visually, this is the slope of the tangent line to our curve at any given moment.

sections.title: The Second Derivative: Acceleration
sections.teaches: The second derivative measures how the rate of change itself is changing (concavity/acceleration).
sections.visual: The scene transitions to a new graph. The previous tangent line's slope values are plotted as a new green curve, f''(t). Arrows indicate that when f'(t) increases, f''(t) is positive; when f'(t) decreases, f''(t) is negative. The original blue curve shows concavity (curving up or down) matching the sign of the green line.
sections.narration: Now we ask: how is velocity changing? The second derivative measures acceleration. If the slope of our original curve is getting steeper, the second derivative is positive; if it's flattening out, it is negative.

sections.title: The Third Derivative: Jerk
sections.teaches: The third derivative represents jerk—the rate of change of acceleration.
sections.visual: A third graph appears below the second. The green f''(t) curve is now differentiated to create a red curve, f'''(t). A slider moves along the time axis; when the green line (acceleration) rises sharply, the red line (jerk) spikes upward. Labels 'Jerk' and 'f'''(t)' are highlighted.
sections.narration: But acceleration doesn't change smoothly in real life. The third derivative, known as jerk, measures how abruptly acceleration changes. High jerk means a sudden, jarring shift in force.

sections.title: Generalization: Higher Orders
sections.teaches: Higher-order derivatives continue this pattern, describing the rate of change of the previous derivative.
sections.visual: A stack of graphs builds up: f(t), f'(t), f''(t), f'''(t), and then a dashed curve for f^(4)(t). Each step shows an arrow labeled 'd/dt' pointing to the next. The sequence fades into a general formula notation: d^n/dx^n. Text appears: 'Mathematical Abstraction'.
sections.narration: We can continue this process indefinitely. Each higher-order derivative describes how the previous rate of change is evolving. While physical interpretations become abstract, the mathematical pattern remains consistent: differentiation applied repeatedly.
